summary: Describes a new series of documents, Best Current Practices, that carry the endorsement of the IESG. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo creates a publication series for Internet practices endorsed by the IETF. It explains how BCPs are reviewed and how they differ from Internet Standards.

questions: what is the best current practice series
can a bcp become an internet standard
what is a best current practice
subtitle: The memo that established the Best Current Practices RFC subseries.

tldr.problem: The IETF had standards-track documents and less formal RFCs, but lacked a publication route for technical guidance carrying IETF endorsement.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1818 establishes the Best Current Practices subseries, reviewed by the IESG with the existing review process and a last call before publication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1818 is Historic. A BCP carries IETF technical approval but cannot become an official Internet Standard.

today: RFC 1818 is marked Historic in the unit metadata, with no replacement recorded. It describes the original creation of the BCP series.

sections.title: A Gap in RFC Publication
sections.content:
The RFC process described in this memo had standards-track documents, which could lead to an official Internet Standard, and other RFCs such as informational, experimental, and FYI documents. Informational RFCs had a less formal publication process and, according to the memo, no significance within the IETF process.

The IETF had no other way to publish relevant technical information that it endorsed. RFC 1818 creates a new subseries to fill that gap.
sections.plainLanguage: The process had formal standards and informal notes, but no category for technical guidance endorsed by the IETF. The BCP series was created for that purpose.

sections.title: Reviewing a Best Current Practice
sections.content:
Documents in the Best Current Practices series carry the endorsement of the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG). The process resembles the proposed-standard process: the IESG reviews the document, including the existing last-call process on the IETF announcement mailing list.

Once the IESG approves a BCP, the process ends and the document is published. The memo gives OSI NSAP allocation and the OSPF applicability statement as possible subjects for BCPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A BCP is reviewed by the IESG, and the community gets a last call to comment. Once approved, it is published without moving through a standards maturity ladder.

sections.title: BCPs and Internet Standards
sections.content:
A published BCP is viewed as having the IETF's technical approval. The memo clearly distinguishes that approval from an official Internet Standard: a BCP is not a standard and cannot become one.

This RFC is itself BCP 1. The unit metadata lists it as Historic and records no replacement RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: A BCP is endorsed technical guidance, not an Internet Standard. The distinction is part of the publication category itself.
